claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater plastic-strain tolerance than pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater toughness than pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading.
Pronounced atomic-scale lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr modifies its dislocation dynamics.
Plasticity in WTaTiVZr shifts toward edge-dislocation dominance rather than the screw-dislocation dominance typical of tungsten.
Lattice distortion or chemical disorder creates a uniform distribution of nanoscale barriers to dislocation motion in WTaTiVZr.
The nanoscale barriers alter the activation-energy landscape and promote edge-dislocation behavior over screw-dislocation behavior.
Edge-dislocation-dominated deformation accelerates dynamic recovery and subgrain formation in WTaTiVZr.
Accelerated dynamic recovery improves the alloy's capacity to accommodate plastic strain and increases toughness.
The initial equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy is homogeneous and single phase.
The refractory HEA phase remains stable throughout the full proposed 800–1200°C test range.
Commercially used pure tungsten can be represented by a single-crystal pure-tungsten comparator.
Under identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will have a lower and more spatially uniform dislocation density than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will have a higher fraction of edge dislocations than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will show earlier subgrain formation than pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten exhibits predominantly screw-dislocation-controlled deformation and less efficient dynamic recovery and subgrain formation under the stated conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically to sustained loading at 800–1200°C under plasma-facing-component service conditions.

Identically loaded WTaTiVZr and pure-tungsten specimens, characterized by neutron diffraction and high-resolution TEM, provide a controlled test of differences in dislocation character, density, and subgrain formation.
